_meta: A run of 30 items partitioned into three chunks of size 10, addressed two ways -- with closed inclusive ranges [start, end] and with half-open ranges [start, end) that exclude their upper bound -- used to show that half-open intervals tile a range without gaps or overlaps while closed intervals double-count the shared boundary and overrun the end. A range needs two numbers, a start and an end, and the only question is whether the end is included. A closed interval [a, b] includes both ends, so two adjacent chunks written [0, 10] and [10, 20] both contain the index 10: the boundary element is double-counted, in two chunks at once. A half-open interval [a, b) includes the start and excludes the end, so [0, 10) and [10, 20) meet exactly at 10 with 10 belonging only to the second: adjacent half-open ranges partition the whole with no element in two chunks and none in none. Half-open intervals also make the arithmetic clean -- the number of integers in [a, b) is exactly b minus a, adjacent chunks are [i*size, (i+1)*size), and concatenating them just works -- which is why Python's range, slicing, and almost every well-designed range API are end-exclusive. n_items is how many items there are (indices 0 to n_items-1); chunk_size is the chunk length. The closed and half-open chunk membership, the double-counted boundaries, the overrun past the end, and whether each scheme partitions the items are computed. Stdlib only.
